opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it came down to the fact that pure next-token prediction gives you a model that's very good at imitating the distribution of text it was trained on, but imitation alone doesn't tell the model what you actually *want*. You end up with something that can continue a document fluently, but it isn't necessarily helpful, or truthful, or following instructions. So there was this gap between "the model knows a lot" and "the model does the right thing with what it knows."

Reinforcement learning was appealing because it lets you supervise at the level of outcomes rather than at the level of individual tokens. Instead of having to write down the exact correct response for every prompt, which is expensive and often ambiguous, you can just say, "this answer is better than that one," and let the model figure out how to move toward the better behavior. That's a much more scalable signal in a lot of ways. Humans are generally much better at judging or comparing outputs than at producing the ideal output themselves.

There's also a historical piece. Many of the people at OpenAI early on came from a reinforcement learning background, robotics, games, Dota, things like that. So RL was a natural lens for them. They thought of the language model as a policy, and once you frame it that way, optimizing it against a reward, whether from human preferences or a learned reward model, feels like the obvious next step.

And I'd add that, from my perspective, it's interesting because it hints at something deeper. RL supervision is essentially a way of giving the model a verifier, a sense of what good looks like, and then letting it search or refine toward that. I think that idea of separating generation from evaluation, and using the evaluator to improve the generator, is one of the more powerful ideas in AI broadly, and it connects to a lot of the work I do on energy-based models and iterative reasoning, where you're explicitly learning a function that scores solutions and then optimizing against it.

r001.rationale: The response says next-token imitation of training text does not teach the model to be helpful, truthful, or follow instructions, and explains that reinforcement learning can steer it toward those desired behaviors through outcome-based feedback.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's worth remembering where a lot of those people came from. A big chunk of the early OpenAI research group had spent years on reinforcement learning — Atari, robotics, Dota — and the whole mental model there is that you have an agent that acts in a world and gets a scalar signal back telling it how well it did. So when language models started getting good enough to be interesting, the natural question for that community was: how do I get this thing to do what I actually want, rather than just predict the next token of internet text?

And pretraining alone doesn't give you a handle on that. You're imitating the data distribution, which includes a lot of things you don't want the model to say or do. There's no notion of "better" or "worse" baked in — just "more likely" or "less likely." RL gives you that missing piece. You can define a reward, even a fuzzy one learned from human preferences, and optimize directly against it. That felt very familiar to people who had spent years thinking about reward functions and policy optimization.

I think there was also a practical appeal. Writing down a loss function for "be helpful and honest" is basically impossible, but having humans compare two outputs and say which one they prefer is something you can actually collect at scale. Learning a reward model from those comparisons and then doing policy gradient on top of it was a very clean way to turn an ill-defined objective into something you could optimize. The RLHF work in the summarization papers and then InstructGPT showed it worked surprisingly well with relatively small amounts of feedback.

And honestly, part of it was a research culture thing. Supervised fine-tuning feels like you're just copying demonstrations. RL feels like the model can discover behaviors that go beyond what the demonstrators showed it — which is what everyone in that community had been chasing since AlphaGo. Whether that promise is fully realized for language is still an open question, but I think that aspiration explains a lot of the early enthusiasm.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining only imitates internet text and provides no signal for what is better or worse, while reinforcement learning lets researchers optimize for desired behavior using rewards or human preferences.

astra-6.text:
I think the appeal was that it’s much easier to judge an answer than to specify exactly how to produce it. With supervised learning, you need someone to write the response you want the model to imitate. But for a lot of questions, there isn’t one correct response. You might have several answers that are all reasonable, but some are more helpful or clearer than others.

Reinforcement learning gives you a way to use that feedback. You can have people compare responses, learn a reward signal from those preferences, and then train the model to produce answers that score better. So you’re moving beyond just predicting what text comes next toward producing something people actually find useful. I think that was a big part of the attraction.

r001.rationale: The response says preference feedback can train models to produce more useful answers, but it does not explain that reinforcement learning was appealing for teaching behaviors difficult to learn from internet text alone.

sol-6.1.text: I think the appeal was that it’s often much easier to judge an answer than to write the ideal answer yourself. If you’re training a language model just to predict text, you’re teaching it to imitate what’s on the internet, which isn’t necessarily the behavior you want from an assistant. With reinforcement learning, you can have people compare responses and say, “This one is more helpful,” and use that feedback to guide the model. So it gave researchers a way to optimize for what people actually preferred, without having to explicitly specify every aspect of a good response.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts imitating internet text with using human preference feedback to guide assistant behavior, explaining why reinforcement learning could teach behavior that text prediction alone would not.
